content.value_statement: Timed captions can be difficult to create and synchronize in video compositions. This skill provides practical guidance for transcribing, importing, formatting, and rendering captions in Remotion.
actual_capabilities: Defines the Caption JSON fields used by Remotion.
Shows how to transcribe audio with @remotion/install-whisper-cpp.
Shows how to save generated captions as a JSON asset.
Shows how to import and parse local SRT subtitle files.
Shows how to fetch local caption assets during rendering.
Explains caption pages, timing, whitespace, and active-word highlighting.
limitations: It provides guidance and examples, not a complete Remotion project.
Audio transcription requires installing the Whisper.cpp integration and its model.
The optional ffmpeg conversion example is commented out and requires local setup.
Caption quality depends on the source audio and the selected transcription model.

use_cases.title: Add captions to a social video
use_cases.description: Create timed caption pages and highlight the active word in a Remotion composition.

use_cases.title: Reuse an existing subtitle file
use_cases.description: Load a local SRT file, parse it, and use the captions with Remotion utilities.

use_cases.title: Transcribe recorded narration
use_cases.description: Generate caption JSON from an audio file with the Remotion Whisper.cpp integration.

prompt_templates.title: Start with caption JSON
prompt_templates.prompt: Show me how to represent these timed subtitles as Remotion Caption JSON: Hello from 0 to 900 milliseconds, then world from 900 to 1500 milliseconds.

prompt_templates.title: Import an SRT file
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me load a local subtitles.srt file from the Remotion public folder and parse it with @remotion/captions.

prompt_templates.title: Render caption pages
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Remotion component that groups Caption data into pages and renders each page at the correct time.

prompt_templates.title: Build a transcription workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a local Remotion workflow that transcribes one audio clip at a time, saves Caption JSON files, and renders synchronized captions.

output_examples.input: I have a local SRT file and need captions in my composition.
output: Place the SRT file in the public folder.
Load it with staticFile and fetch it during rendering.
Parse the text with parseSrt, then pass the captions to Remotion caption utilities.

output_examples.input: I want a TikTok-style caption display.
output: Group captions into pages with createTikTokStyleCaptions.
Render each page in a timed Sequence.
Use token timestamps to color the word currently being spoken.

best_practices: Store each clip's captions in a separate local JSON file.
Keep spaces in caption token text and use whiteSpace: pre when rendering.
Test page timing at the composition frame rate before exporting a video.
anti_patterns: Do not use caption text without timing data for synchronized rendering.
Do not remove leading spaces from tokenized captions when word spacing matters.
Do not assume one transcription model produces accurate captions for every audio source.

faq.question: What caption format does this skill use?
faq.answer: It uses the Remotion Caption format with text, start time, end time, timestamp, and confidence fields.

faq.question: Can I use an existing SRT file?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill shows how to fetch a local SRT asset and parse it with parseSrt.

faq.question: Can the skill transcribe audio?
faq.answer: It explains how to use the Remotion Whisper.cpp integration to transcribe audio and convert the result to captions.

faq.question: Where should I save caption files?
faq.answer: Save local caption JSON or SRT assets where your Remotion project can serve them as static files.

faq.question: Does it support word highlighting?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows how to use caption token timing to identify and style the active word.

faq.question: Does it install dependencies automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides installation commands and implementation guidance, but you run commands in your own project.
